extracted.intended_audience: inventors and first-time applicants preparing a US (USPTO) patent application
extracted.subtask_description: Step-by-step practical guidance for preparing and filing a patent application at the USPTO, including assessing patentability, drafting specification/drawings/claims, filing choices, prosecution, and maintenance. Aimed at inventors considering DIY or initial preparation before counsel review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Your invention must be (a) patentable subject matter (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter), (b) new (not anticipated by prior art), (c) useful, and (d) non-obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your invention is a pure mathematical algorithm, a law of nature, or an abstract idea, it likely fails subject matter eligibility. Treat each prong (subject matter, novelty, utility, non-obviousness) as a separate threshold to evaluate before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document the invention thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a complete description of the invention before talking to attorneys. Include: what it does, how it works, what makes it different from existing solutions, alternative versions, and best results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Date and witness the document. Provide enough detail to enable practice by a person skilled in the art and to support later claim scope and priority; disclose multiple embodiments and best modes where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct a prior art search
rubrics_metrics.description: Search the USPTO patent database, Google Patents, Espacenet, and academic literature. Look for patents and publications in the same technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to find references that disclose anything similar (anticipation or relevant prior art for obviousness). Use these results to shape claim scope and specification disclosures; document search strategy and key references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide provisional vs non-provisional filing
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional is cheaper and faster but does not get examined. A non-provisional starts the prosecution clock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most applicants file provisional first, then convert within 12 months. Remember a provisional establishes a filing date but does not mature into a patent without a later non‑provisional filing; plan conversion/timing and content to support desired claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification structure and required sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections in order: Title, Cross-References, Field of Invention, Background, Summary, Brief Description of Drawings, Detailed Description, Claims, Abstract. Each section has a specific purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the conventional order and give each section its intended content (e.g., Background describes prior art/problems; Summary outlines invention; Detailed Description enables practice). Use the specification to support claim scope and alternatives; avoid over-limiting language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent drawings formatting and linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drawings have specific format requirements (37 CFR 1.84): black ink, specific paper size, margins, line weights, lettering size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each element in the spec should be reference-numbered to a corresponding feature in a drawing. Follow 37 CFR 1.84 for line weights, margins, paper, and lettering; use figures generously to illustrate embodiments and alternatives; ensure numbers in drawings match the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting fundamentals
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are the legal definition of the invention. Independent claims stand alone; dependent claims add limitations to a parent claim. Use specific transitional phrases ("comprising," "consisting of"). Each claim is a single sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft independent claims to capture the broadest allowable invention, and dependent claims to add fallback limitations. Choose transitional language carefully (e.g., "comprising" is open-ended, "consisting of" is closed). Ensure each claim is written as one properly punctuated sentence and is supported by the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing procedure and required documents
rubrics_metrics.description: File electronically through Patent Center. Pay filing, search, and examination fees (reduced for small entity, micro entity). Include the specification, drawings, claims, abstract, oath/declaration, and assignment if applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use USPTO Patent Center for electronic filing; confirm entity status for fee reductions and include all required parts (oath/declaration, assignments). Check fee amounts and proper forms to avoid processing delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to Office Actions (prosecution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO will likely issue an office action with rejections. Respond within the deadline (usually 3 months, extendable to 6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare amendments and arguments to overcome rejections; consider strategic claim amendments or persuasive arguments on novelty/non-obviousness or claim interpretation. Track deadlines carefully and use available extensions when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance, issue fee, and post-issuance maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: If allowed, pay the issue fee within 3 months. After issuance, pay maintenance fees at 3.5, 7.5, and 11.5 years to keep the patent in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor allowance notices and pay issue fee on time to obtain the patent. Plan for periodic maintenance fees (and associated surcharges if late) to preserve enforceability; understand fee schedule and entity status effects on fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical drafting and disclosure tips for beginners
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the words "essential" or "critical" in the spec. Disclose multiple ways to practice the invention. Use figures generously. Have a patent attorney review even if you are filing pro se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid language that may unduly limit claim scope (e.g., labeling features as essential). Broadly disclose alternative embodiments and implementation options to support claim breadth. Produce helpful figures. Even non-lawyers should seek attorney review before final filing to catch legal pitfalls.
